solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Flagon of beer as conveyed by Spooner to dance

indicators.note: Dr Spooner swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so the phrase must be said his way

blocks.note: a jug of bitter, the British beer, with its first sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A tankard of ale passes through the hands of a famously tongue-tied clergyman on its way to a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British pale ale; a jug holds it. Swap the B and J sounds of BITTER JUG to get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The jitterbug is a lively swing dance popular in the 1930s and 1940s, so it is an example of a dance.

clue.text: Politician and celebrity involved in project get going

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to sit inside it, so the first two pieces go within the third

explanation.surface: A politician and a famous name join some project to get it moving.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump-start an engine or a scheme is to kick it into action quickly, the same as getting it going.

clue.text: Reprimand, not very loud, and very short, for idling

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to leave the following letters out of the reprimand
something short has lost its end, so the word for very is cut down

explanation.surface: A quiet, brief telling-off given to someone for being lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: Take FF (fortissimo, very loud) out of TICKING OFF, then add VER(y).
explanation.definitionFit: An engine ticking over runs slowly without doing work, which is exactly what idling means.

clue.text: Tips for office job: do no donkey-work and no paperwork!

definitions.text: Tips for office job: do no donkey-work and no paperwork!

indicators.note: the tips of words are their extremities; here the tail ends are wanted

explanation.surface: Advice for an office worker: avoid drudgery and avoid all the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letters of the five words before 'and' spell the answer, and the whole clue describes a book that needs no paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic book is read on a screen, so it involves no printed pages at all.

clue.text: Bedroom at first holding advantage over study

indicators.note: 'at first' points to the opening letter of the room

blocks.note: being one up is having an edge over a rival
on top of, as in 'on the table'

explanation.surface: Someone in the bedroom keeps an edge by doing extra study.
explanation.definitionFit: To bone up on a subject is informal for revising or cramming it, which is to study it.

clue.text: Scoff when crossword’s abandoned quietly for good

indicators.note: the soft letter is abandoned and the good one takes its place
'for' means in place of, telling us one letter replaces another

explanation.surface: Someone eats greedily once they quietly give up on the crossword for good.
explanation.walkthrough: In PUZZLE, P (piano) is swapped for G.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff food is to eat it greedily, which is just what guzzling means.

clue.text: Novelist’s oddly set view lacks moral, ultimately

indicators.note: something done oddly is done in a strange way, so these letters come out rearranged
'ultimately' picks the very last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A critic says a novelist's strangely fixed outlook is missing any moral.
explanation.definitionFit: Vita Sackville-West was an English novelist and poet, author of The Edwardians and All Passion Spent.

clue.text: Format for golf talk arranged with pro? Yes

indicators.note: the letters are arranged afresh into a new order

explanation.surface: A golfer asks a professional whether a chat about the competition's format has been set up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the fodder words; all of talk, pro and yes are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroke play is the golf competition format where total shots over the round decide the winner, unlike match play.

clue.text: Getting fit again, do trail across glen

indicators.note: the trail is laid across the valley, stretching round it

blocks.note: to do someone is to swindle them
a scent is the trail a hound follows

explanation.surface: Instructions for a recovery hike: follow a path across a Scottish valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' here is slang for cheat, not a verb of action; the trail is the scent a hound follows, laid round the valley.
explanation.definitionFit: A convalescent person is recovering after illness, regaining health, so getting fit again fits as an adjective.

clue.text: Thick aristocrat trading books for seconds

indicators.note: trading one thing for another means swapping them, so one pair of letters is exchanged

blocks.note: a nobleman ranking below an earl

explanation.surface: A dim nobleman swaps his reading matter for second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: The NT at the end of VISCOUNT is replaced by S.
explanation.definitionFit: A viscous liquid is thick and sticky, flowing slowly like syrup.

clue.text: Coffee time’s about right? Isn’t for a Mormon

indicators.note: 'about' puts the coffee and time around the abbreviation for right

blocks.note: a day is a period of time, with the 's

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a coffee break is acceptable for a member of a church that shuns caffeine.
explanation.walkthrough: Mormons are taught to avoid coffee, which gives the question its sting.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are popularly called Mormons.

clue.text: Oriental drama used to be turned to Victorian satire

indicators.note: turned round, so the combined letters are read from the back

explanation.surface: An Eastern play has been adapted into a nineteenth-century satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oriental' is not E here; it describes the drama, which is Japanese Noh.
explanation.definitionFit: Erewhon is Samuel Butler's 1872 satirical novel about a utopia, its title nearly nowhere spelt backwards.

clue.text: State official left inside hears alarm going off

indicators.note: 'inside' places the letter for left among the other letters
an alarm going off is set off, and the letters are set off into a new order

explanation.surface: A government figure, left indoors, hears an alarm ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl Marshal is a great officer of state in England who organises state ceremonies like coronations.

clue.text: Nurse could take this work through agency?

blocks.note: first meaning: a short form of temperature, which a nurse measures
second meaning: to do short-term jobs arranged by an employment agency

explanation.surface: A nurse wonders whether to take a job found through a staffing agency.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests agency nursing, but the first part is about taking a patient's temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal both for a body temperature reading and for doing temporary office work.

clue.text: Lens for camera cases returned

indicators.note: the words encase the answer, holding it within their letters
returned means sent back, so the letters are read right to left

explanation.surface: A photographer sends back a lens bought for a camera, with its cases.
explanation.definitionFit: A macro lens is a camera lens designed for extreme close-up photography of small subjects.

clue.text: Early Christians sneakily ensnare a leader of Zionism

indicators.note: acting sneakily means being devious, so the letters are deviously rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter, at the front of the line

explanation.surface: First-century believers lay a trap for a Zionist leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Nazarenes was an early name for followers of Jesus of Nazareth, used for the first Christians.

clue.text: Boy fronting pupils’ moving proposition

blocks.note: rapid eye movement, the darting of the pupils during dreaming sleep

explanation.surface: A boy at the head of a class of pupils makes a proposal that stirs them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupils' are those of the eye, not schoolchildren: REM stands for rapid eye movement.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a theorem is a proposition proved from axioms, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Endure a bitter little general harbouring fancy project, obviously

annotation.answer: STICK OUT LIKE A SORE THUMB

indicators.note: a harbour shelters ships within it, so the word for fancy sits inside the rest

blocks.note: to stick something out is to put up with it
General Tom Thumb, the tiny showman of P T Barnum's circus

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with a resentful small-time commander who is nursing a pet scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for the bitter little general is split open after the endurance phrase to take in the word for fancy. General Tom Thumb was a famously short American performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that sticks out like a sore thumb projects so conspicuously that everyone notices it.

clue.text: Country no longer could come to hero’s aid

indicators.note: the letters could come to something else once rearranged

explanation.surface: A fallen nation might come to the rescue of a champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia was the name of the state now called Zimbabwe, so it is a country that no longer exists.

clue.text: Boy soon getting around large resistance

indicators.note: the word for soon gets around the others, enclosing them

explanation.surface: A lad will soon overcome a lot of opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: LGE is the standard short form of large, as on shop labels.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon is a boy's name, as borne by Algernon Moncrieff in The Importance of Being Earnest.

clue.text: Discharging energy again going through stocks

indicators.note: to stock something is to hold it, so the outer word holds the letter for energy

explanation.surface: Energy is released again as it passes through the stocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocks' looks like a noun for shares or a pillory but is a verb meaning holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Relieving someone of a duty discharges them from it, as relieving a sentry ends their watch.

clue.text: Did like eating vegetables, becoming satisfied

indicators.note: something eaten goes inside the eater, so the vegetables go within

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed eating their greens and ended up content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did like' looks like enjoyed, but means copied.
explanation.definitionFit: Appeased means pacified by having demands met, which is a sense of satisfied.

clue.text: Pole appearing earlier in Gdansk

blocks.note: surface reading: a Polish person who turned up first in the port city
setter's reading: one of the two magnetic poles, whose initial letter comes before the other's in the spelling of Gdansk

explanation.surface: A Polish citizen arrived in the Baltic port before everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: In GDANSK the letter N stands before S, so the pole abbreviated N appears earlier in the word than the pole abbreviated S.
explanation.definitionFit: The north pole is one of the two poles, the one written as N, so the answer names that pole.

clue.text: Yanks holding Republican line in mess

indicators.note: the yanking word holds the other two letters within it

blocks.note: to hoick is to pull or jerk

explanation.surface: Americans are holding to the party line while in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yanks' looks like Americans but is the verb jerks. Horlicks is a malted milk drink, and in British slang to make a Horlicks of something is to make a mess of it.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the brand name as a euphemism for a botched job or a mess.

clue.text: Note first of series of books portraying Italian town

blocks.note: seventh note of the sol-fa scale
volume one, the first in a set of books

explanation.surface: A short note introduces the first volume in a series depicting a town in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of series' looks like a request for an initial letter, but it means the first volume, VOL I.
explanation.definitionFit: Tivoli is a town near Rome known for the Villa d'Este and Hadrian's Villa.

clue.text: Host clutching very large and fine decoration

indicators.note: the host clutches the other pieces, holding them within

blocks.note: A1, first-class, written with the letter I for the figure one

explanation.surface: A party host is holding on to some very big and delicate ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosaic is a decorative picture made of small coloured tiles, a form of ornamentation.

clue.text: Plant arrived at by pilot carpeted with gold

blocks.note: to pilot a plane is to fly it
old past tense of chide; to be carpeted is to be told off

explanation.surface: A plant reached by an airman who was reprimanded and given gold.
explanation.walkthrough: To carpet someone is British slang for to reprimand them, and chid is an archaic past form of chide.
explanation.definitionFit: The fly orchid is a European wild orchid whose flowers look like insects.

clue.text: Lover one day turned up with a Disney film

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A sweetheart showed up one day with a cartoon classic.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantasia is Disney's 1940 animated feature set to classical music.

clue.text: Bothered following leads that brave folk wouldn’t?

indicators.note: 'following' puts the word for bothered after the word for leads, reversing their clue order

blocks.note: to lead an organisation is to run it
to be bothered about something is to care

explanation.surface: Someone troubled by a set of clues does what a bold person never would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads' is a verb, as in leads a team. The definition reads with the answer as 'run scared, which brave folk would not'.
explanation.definitionFit: To run scared is to flee in fear, behaviour the courageous would never show.

clue.text: Translated first, sign small, compact novel

blocks.note: Aries, a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A short novel that was first translated, with a small signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristram Shandy is Laurence Sterne's comic eighteenth-century novel, famous for its digressions.

clue.text: Some biscuits and bread carried out by one on plane

definitions.text: carried out by one on plane

blocks.note: a biscuit barrel is the jar some biscuits are kept in

explanation.surface: Snacks of biscuits and bread being served by someone on a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: A biscuit barrel is the British name for a cookie jar.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel roll is an aerobatic manoeuvre that a pilot performs, rolling the aircraft through a full spiral.

clue.text: Ace hobby, training to become lifeguard

indicators.note: training reshapes things, so these letters are reshaped into a new word

explanation.surface: Someone's great pastime is practising to qualify as a lifesaver.
explanation.definitionFit: A beach boy can be a young man employed on a beach, often as an attendant or lifesaver.

clue.text: Party to open pub with ball…

indicators.note: the pub is opened up so that something can be put inside

explanation.surface: A party is starting up at the pub, with a dance to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to the next clue, where the ball continues as a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in on a plan is to be party to it, sharing its secret.

clue.text: …Ring to cancel our party

explanation.surface: The ball from the previous clue becomes a phone call to call off the party.
explanation.definitionFit: An annulus is a ring-shaped figure, the region between two concentric circles.

clue.text: Appropriate to give maiden an indispensable partner

blocks.note: to hand something over is to give it

explanation.surface: It seems proper to offer a young woman an essential companion.
explanation.walkthrough: M for maiden comes from cricket scorecards, where a maiden is an over with no runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A right-hand man is a trusted chief assistant someone cannot do without.

clue.text: Depressions drastically increase militancy of mining unions?

blocks.note: to arm a group is to make it ready for fighting
a pit is a coal mine, and the question mark admits the stretch from mines to their workforces

explanation.surface: A call for coal miners' unions to become far more combative.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as an instruction to 'arm pits': to make the mines militant. The hollows meant are those under the shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: The armpits are the hollows under the arms, physical depressions in the body.

clue.text: Reminder of passing minutes — no more time, sadly

indicators.note: the words are sadly mangled, so their letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A bleak note that the minutes have run out and time is gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation for minutes joins the rest of the letters in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A memento mori, Latin for remember you must die, is an object that reminds us of death.

clue.text: Change from upright character into criminal

indicators.note: 'into' places the upright letter within the criminal

blocks.note: a letter that stands straight up

explanation.surface: An honest person turns into a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like a verb but is the noun for loose money. 'upright character' sounds like an honest person; it is the straight-standing letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Change means small money, and a coin is a single piece of it.

clue.text: Periodical not available to convey a historic document

explanation.surface: A magazine cannot be found to carry an old charter.
explanation.definitionFit: Magna Carta is the charter of rights sealed by King John in 1215, a famous historical text.

clue.text: Draw in study period that’s not specially tailored

indicators.note: 'in' puts the drawing word inside the period

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: A sketch made during a stint of study that was not specially commissioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-to-wear clothes are made in standard sizes and sold off the peg, not made to measure.

clue.text: My Greek food company not touching alcohol

explanation.surface: Someone describes their Greek restaurant business that serves no drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is not a possessive here but the exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated exclamations of astonishment, used interchangeably to express surprise.

clue.text: During vacation, lass meeting Irish Americans in neighbourhood?

indicators.note: something during a holiday falls within it, so the girl and Irish go inside

explanation.surface: On holiday, a girl gets acquainted with some local Irish-Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: Hols is British slang for holidays.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang homegirls are female friends from one's own area, hence the question mark.

clue.text: What widow would give not to end a recluse

indicators.note: 'not to end' means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: in the Gospel parable, the poor widow gave her mite, a tiny coin

explanation.surface: A widow wonders what she should donate so as not to finish up alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The widow's mite, from Mark's Gospel, was the small coin a poor widow gave; HER MITE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit lives apart from society, so the word is a direct synonym for a recluse.

clue.text: Bring up something one’s pinned to one’s ear

indicators.note: what reaches one's ear is a sound, so we want a word that sounds like the jewellery

blocks.note: a brooch is a pinned ornament

explanation.surface: Raising the subject of an earring someone has pinned on.
explanation.definitionFit: To broach a topic is to raise or introduce it in conversation.

clue.text: Swindled punter ought to

blocks.note: to be had is to be tricked

explanation.surface: A gambler who has been cheated should do something about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A punter is British for a gambler.
explanation.definitionFit: You had better do something means you should or ought to do it.

clue.text: Family’s experiences near a city in Africa

explanation.surface: A family's adventures near an African city.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinshasa is the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a large city in Africa.

clue.text: Had perished at sea, in doctor’s absence

indicators.note: the doctor is absent, so the letters for a doctor are removed

explanation.surface: A sailor died at sea because no doctor was on board.
explanation.definitionFit: To have something is to own it, so had and owned are past-tense synonyms.

clue.text: In the main, SAE speeds up packages

indicators.note: the words package the answer, wrapping it inside their letters
in a down entry, up means the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Mostly, a stamped addressed envelope gets parcels moving faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly' but means at sea, the main being the ocean. An SAE is a stamped addressed envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is a poetic word for the open ocean, so something in the main is out at sea, in deep water.

clue.text: Boy needs mum: is that unusual?

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement of these letters is wanted

explanation.surface: A little boy wanting his mother, and someone asking whether that is odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthias is a boy's name, borne by the apostle chosen to replace Judas.

clue.text: Variable illustration featuring in short story classic

indicators.note: the story is cut short, losing its last letter
a thing featuring in something appears within it

explanation.surface: A picture appearing in a brief story collection that has become a classic.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic example of something is a typical one, showing its characteristic features.

clue.text: Impracticable cunning failed to get a hearing

indicators.note: the phrase is heard rather than seen, so we want what sounds like it

blocks.note: wile is cunning, and to die is to fail

explanation.surface: A clever scheme fell through because nobody would listen to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild-eyed scheme is extreme and unrealistic, so the adjective fits ideas that are impracticable.

clue.text: Pudding is where you’ll get tea, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the location phrase becomes a word

blocks.note: tea is the letter T, whose place in the alphabet is right behind the letter S

explanation.surface: Dessert is served where you can have a cup of tea, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea is the letter T, which follows S in the alphabet. Afters is British for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is informal British for pudding, the course that comes after the main dish.

clue.text: And so send them to sleep in just a pyjama jacket?

definitions.text: And so send them to sleep in just a pyjama jacket?

blocks.clueFragment: And so send them to sleep
blocks.note: setter's reading: be so dull that listeners nod off
surface reading: someone has lost the bottom half of their nightwear, so the trousers have been taken away

explanation.surface: Someone is put to bed wearing only a pyjama top.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for being utterly tedious is taken literally: the victim has had the trousers removed and sleeps in the top alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To bore the pants off someone is an idiom for being extremely tedious to them, enough to make them doze.

clue.text: Laconic admission from groom sounded pitiful

blocks.note: the terse first word of a man owning up

explanation.surface: A tight-lipped bridegroom confesses that he is married.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue imagines a groom's clipped confession 'Me wed', a two-word sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To mew is to make a thin cat-like cry, a plaintive and pitiful sound.

clue.text: Drink bottles beginning to contaminate fish

indicators.note: the drink bottles up a letter, holding it inside
the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A drink holds the beginnings of contamination of the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The scup is a porgy, an edible fish of the American Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Popular novelist doesn’t stop interfering with books?

blocks.note: to cook the books is to falsify accounts

explanation.surface: A best-selling author keeps fiddling with the accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook the books is an idiom for falsifying accounts; COOKS ON then means keeps doing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine Cookson was one of the most borrowed and best-selling British novelists of the twentieth century.

clue.text: I run in, this time

indicators.note: 'in' tells us the first two pieces go inside a third

blocks.note: the punctuation mark that follows the word in, standing for its own name

explanation.surface: Someone reports going for a jog, then says it is about now.
explanation.walkthrough: The mark after 'in' is itself part of the wordplay: one and run go into the comma, a self-referential trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the neutral name for the calendar epoch we are living in now, the present time.

clue.text: Extract from a little white lie

blocks.note: the abbreviation for white, a little of the word
to lie down is to rest

explanation.surface: Pulling out a small fib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'white lie' wants to be read as a fib; split it, and lie is the verb for resting.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrest something is to pull it out forcibly, so it means to extract.

clue.text: Mir apparently going around the earth, for example

indicators.note: letters going around get spun into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The Mir space station seems to be orbiting our planet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's orbiting space station distracts from the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A primary planet orbits the sun directly, unlike a moon; our own world is one such body.

clue.text: One traducing Solicitor at Law: and before king!

explanation.surface: A lawyer in court and in front of the monarch is accused of smearing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To traduce is to speak badly of someone falsely, which is what a slanderer does.
